links.reason: Same title செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் goes to grace and to hearing, and 411 adds 'chief of all wealths', so the wording pulls apart even though Parimelazhagar reconciles it by reading each against material wealth only.

விழுச்செல்வம் names not-wanting (none equal in either world) and learning (all else is not wealth), a real rivalry in wording that Parimelazhagar eases by limiting 400's 'others' to gems and gold; the note's 'not a doctrine' is inference.

Both demote material property, but 592 uses a different title (உடைமை) and its stated foil is பொருளுடைமை only, so with Parimelazhagar's gems-and-gold on 400 they only share the topic and the note's 'sole true possession' is not a clash.

400 says things other than learning are not wealth and 751 says nothing but wealth counts for anything, a direct clash on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's readings of 751 (Pope's narrower gloss eases it), though the note errs in citing 'each book's register' since both verses are in the Book of Wealth.
Reversed duplicate of 241-411 with the same relation: identical formula, two holders, reconciled only by reading the foil as material wealth, so it adds no independent evidence.
The ஆக்கம்/ஊங்கு formula truly recurs, but restraint is a species of virtue and 'none greater' allows ties, so the two are compatible and only the shared form is real.

32 allows no gain above virtue while 644 allows neither virtue nor gain above apt speech, which pulls apart on the wording; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar reconcile it by treating speech as cause of virtue, as the note says.

Nothing beats truth in 300 but 323 places not killing first and truth behind it, and Parimelazhagar on 323 explicitly raises this doubt and settles it by the later verse overriding, so this is an acknowledged clash.
92 ranks speech over giving and 225 ranks relieving hunger over enduring it, comparisons that chain without conflict, and the 'hungry person's view' is the note's own speculation.

841 calls lack of understanding the worst lack and says the world does not count want of wealth as lack, against 1041's unmatched misery of poverty; the different scales (worth versus pain) ease but do not remove the pull.

1041 says nothing pains like poverty (Parimelazhagar: no equal, so none greater) and 558 names something that pains more, a literal contradiction limited only by 558's condition of tyranny, with no commentator reconciling it.
An unconditional ban on taking life meets the king's killing likened to weeding, a real conflict on the verses that Parimelazhagar resolves only through royal caste duty at 550.
Reversed duplicate of 327-550, and its statement that Parimelazhagar uses caste duty, which the verses lack, checks out against his note on 550.

Only the word ஒறுத்தல் is shared: 314 concerns one's response to those who wronged oneself and 550 a ruler's punishment of public criminals, so the conflict vanishes in context (the corpus's Parimelazhagar entry for 314 is also misaligned).

303 says forget anger toward anyone and 487 has wise kings seethe inwardly until the time is right on Parimelazhagar's reading, a real pull, though Manakkudavar glosses 487 without stored anger and Parimelazhagar directs 303 at renunciants.

On Manakkudavar's reading the spy wears the ascetic's guise that 274 condemns, and the note rightly scopes this because Parimelazhagar prefers actual renunciant conduct and reports the guise reading as another's; agents differ but the act matches.

Same word ஒப்புரவு: 220 accepts ruin from it as worth selling oneself and 480 warns it destroys wealth without measure, and Parimelazhagar on 480 says even this must not be excessive, so it limits rather than fully reverses.

34 makes a stainless mind all of virtue and 829 prescribes outward friendship with inward killing, and Parimelazhagar concedes duplicity is improper but allowed against enemies, so the note is accurate and the conflict is reconciled by him.

Pun on பற்று: 506 distrusts those without kin ties (Parimelazhagar) or conduct (Manakkudavar) when appointing men and 349 concerns liberation, and both can be true of the same person, so nothing clashes.

Parimelazhagar on 531 is reported correctly, but saying anger may also hit the enemy does not deny that it kills its holder, and 305 never calls anger the worst, so 'demoted' overstates a mere comparison.
Same five sense-objects, but both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar confine 343 to those seeking release and 1101 is a lover's exclamation, so the contrast is real and the clash disappears in context.
Reversed duplicate of 343-1101, and its own 'each its place in different books' concedes that these address different situations rather than conflict.

1017 describes what the shame-ruled would do and 1251 is a woman's lament that desire has broken her reserve, with நாண் here tied to concealing feeling, so this is contrast without incompatibility and 'the whole book depends on it' is flourish.

நிறை is chastity held in the heart in 57 but composure that hides inner feeling in Parimelazhagar's 1251, and her longing for her own husband breaches nothing in 57, so 'inner guard isn't sufficient' does not follow.

The tightest love link: 1017 will not give up shame to save life, and 1132 sets shame aside because body and life cannot bear it, an exact inverse, though Parimelazhagar shows it as a lover's pressure on the maid rather than a revised ethic.

The identical phrase உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு is a bond parted as easily as a bird leaves its egg in 338 and an inseparable union in 1122, and Parimelazhagar glosses them oppositely, calling 338's நட்பு ironic, with no reconciliation offered.

1141's அலர் is town rumour about lovers, not the two-faced backbiting of 183, and 1141 does not commend the gossips, so one verse judges the speaker's life and the other reports a side effect on its subject.
The warrior-undone-by-beauty image works, but 774 never claims invincibility, so this is contrast between a heroic scene and a love conceit with nothing incompatible.

926 charges drink with loss of sense while 1201 only uses liquor's pleasure as a standard of comparison, so a thing can be pleasant and ruinous and the note itself admits there is no judgement to conflict.

Close verbal echo (பின் செல்லா/பின் சென்று), and Parimelazhagar glosses those free of love-sickness as people of honour, so 1255 really does declare 966's ideal unavailable; the note's 'not refuted' correctly marks this as a limit, not a contradiction.
906 faults fear and subservience to a wife, not intimacy, so 'the books value the same intimacy in opposite ways' misreads its target and only the shoulder image is shared.

610 says the sloth-free king gains all that was strode (not 'sleepless'), and 1103 weighs pleasure against the heaven ascetics reach (Manakkudavar says Indra's), so neither sovereignty against sleep nor one shared realm is in view.

Both use நோனா உடம்பு, and on Parimelazhagar's speakers he drops shame while she hangs between shame and love, a real contrast, but the book does not 'state it directly', and her shame also breaks at 1251; 1137 is the direct statement.

The note's condition is honest, yet Manakkudavar gives 1268 to the woman, which erases the contrast (Parimelazhagar names and rejects that view), and anticipating return versus suffering absence is a difference of situation rather than of sex.

No pain in remembering versus remembering burns is a direct clash within one chapter, and Parimelazhagar's attribution (man, then woman) is accurately reported, though Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman, leaving the clash but removing the gender contrast.
மறப்பறியேன் is truly shared and the speakers differ on Parimelazhagar's assignment, but the two do not conflict, and 'clever smile' and 'banter' are the note's additions.
True and nearly trivial: long nights hurt apart and are welcome together, and the note's own wording ('whether the other person is there') shows the variable is presence, not gender.

Both address the moon and the note fits Parimelazhagar on 1210, but he speaks in union praising her face and she speaks in separation, and Manakkudavar reads 1210 differently, so this is a shared addressee rather than a clash.
Parimelazhagar does gloss உள்ளம் as ஊக்கம், but her complaint disputes nothing in 591, and this cross-book pair is not a man-woman contrast within the Book of Love as the thread claims.

759's advice and 1230's cost are compatible statements on wealth-seeking (Parimelazhagar on 'wealth became his nature' is accurate), so the pairing is an affecting juxtaposition rather than a conflict, and it also falls outside the Book of Love.

91 defines sweet speech as free of படிறு, which Parimelazhagar equates with truthfulness, and his 292 counts faultless beneficial falsehood as truth, so on his reading nothing 91 excludes is allowed and the topics merely adjoin.

Unbroken not-lying against conditional falsehood pulls apart on the wording, and Parimelazhagar's definition at 291-292 is what makes them consistent, exactly as the note says, so the conflict is real and internally reconciled.
291 defines one virtue and 200 forbids a different fault, and both can be obeyed together, so 'different standards for speech' mistakes two rules for two answers to one question.
Same pair as in competing_supremes, and relevant here because Parimelazhagar on 323 explains truth's lower rank by its shifting with effect, the thread's own definition.

The echo பொய்யா விளக்கு/விளக்கம் is real, but பொய்யா means not-lying in 299 and unfailing in 753 (Parimelazhagar: நந்தா) and the darks differ (ignorance, enmity), so 'deliberately' is unverifiable and the type would be same_image.

Verse 1 makes no moral claim about the First One and 1062 is a conditional curse (Manakkudavar: better to die than beg), so the point rests on 1062 alone and 'without reservation' adds nothing that verse 1 says.

377 accepts what the apportioner apportions and 1062 curses the world's maker if begging was so decreed, and Parimelazhagar really does describe the same figure assigning livelihood by past deeds; the conditional leaves the conflict open.

Both touch destitution but 330 reports a causal view of disease and poverty while 1062 is about begging as decreed, and Parimelazhagar's 1062 cites past deeds too, so 'refuses to accept it at all' overreads.

Adjacent verses: 169 finds prosperity of the crooked and ruin of the upright a matter to ponder and 170 says neither ever happens, a real pull that Parimelazhagar reconciles with 'if they occur' and past deeds, which the note omits.

Parimelazhagar's 210 says the non-doer of evil has no ruin (அருமை as இன்மை) and 169 treats the upright man's ruin as a fact to ponder; the note's 'absent or rare' is fair and his past-deeds answer at 169 is the reconciliation.

On Parimelazhagar's 377 the apportioner dispenses each soul's own deeds, so austerity (a deed) and apportionment work together, and the 'moral versus fatal' cause dissolves, while Kalaignar reads 270 differently again.

A real inconsistency in Parimelazhagar, whom the note names correctly: on 63 a son's good deeds bring wealth to his parents, on 377 a deed's fruit never goes to another soul; it holds at commentator level only, as the note says.

371 makes effort a product of fate and 620 has effort put fate behind one, a direct conflict stated plainly by Manakkudavar on both, and Parimelazhagar narrows 620 by limiting fate to one or two blockings.

Nothing is stronger than fate versus the persistent see its back is the book's clearest clash, and the note's report of Parimelazhagar narrowing it (fate blocks only a few attempts) is accurate, so it is sound though reconciled by him.

The 'causal arrow reverses' is a logical error: fate gives steadfastness (371) and steadfastness draws wealth (594) form one chain, and Parimelazhagar's 371 calls effort a subsidiary cause, so only the word அசைவு is shared.

மடி comes from adverse fate in 371 and is something one removes in 609 with faults following it out, a real conflict on agency despite 'at will' being stronger than the verse, and no commentator here reconciles them.

The echo தான் முந்துறும் is exact and the contrast real, but neither verse lets human planning beat the unseen power, and Parimelazhagar's 1023 even ties the god's lead to நியதி, so it is an echo rather than incompatibility.

Fate outruns any devised remedy in 380 while foresight spares one from shock in 429, and Manakkudavar on 429 does allow that guarding softens what comes from past deeds, which the note reports correctly as reconciling.

What is not yours will not stay however guarded, and Parimelazhagar says wealth's holding does not depend on care, against timing as a rope binding fleeting wealth, a direct clash with no commentator reconciling it here.
Parimelazhagar's 377 says effort can produce but not enjoy without fate and 619 guarantees a wage for effort, which fit together, and the note itself concedes they 'may coexist'.
370 concerns release through dropping craving and 380 closes a chapter on fate; the drama comes from their position in the book, and neither verse addresses the other's claim.
The word இன்மை is shared, but the ascetic's chosen possessionlessness and involuntary destitution are different conditions, as the note itself says, so the conflict goes away.

இளி appears in both: poverty is no disgrace to one with சால்பு, yet it draws degraded speech even from the well-born, a real pull though the subjects differ (character versus birth) and Parimelazhagar limits 1044 to an occasional lapse.

Parimelazhagar on 408 says poverty does not ruin the good while 532's wording has daily want kill understanding, but the note omits that he glosses 532 as loss of esteem through begging, which largely reconciles them.
Choosing painful poverty over tainted wealth does not deny that poverty is the most painful, so as the note half admits the two are complementary and the tension type is wrong.

A clean clash the note spots correctly: everyone despises those with nothing (752) against the world not counting want of wealth as want (841), and at least one must be normative, with no reconciliation in the commentaries read.
Ideal and report are compatible, as the note says, and Parimelazhagar's reason at 1046 (people avoid hearing the poor lest they be obliged) shows a social fact, not a rival claim about understanding.

959 makes speech the reliable sign of lineage and 1044 has poverty produce base speech from the well-born, so the signal fails as the note says, though Parimelazhagar treats it as an occasional lapse.

Integrity natural only to the well-born against birth alike for all with distinction from deeds pulls apart on the verses; Kalaignar does reverse 951 as stated, and Parimelazhagar's 972 keeps varna work-differences, so 972 denies less on his reading.
Good birth as one requirement for trusted appointment and learning outranking birth in dignity answer different questions, as the note concedes in saying 'can be squared'.

793 and 794 use family as a criterion for choosing friends while 972, especially on Manakkudavar's reading, says greatness is not known by lineage, a real if practical pull; no commentator here addresses it.

Birth is named as one of courtesy's two sources against 972, and the note reports Parimelazhagar's conduct gloss correctly, though its 'a chapter later' is wrong (chapter 98 to chapter 100); reconciled by him, not by Manakkudavar.
Both argue against birth-rank, so the type should be agrees rather than tension, and the note can only say the arguments differ in kind.

On Parimelazhagar's reading the rider and bearer show the fruit of virtue, so distinction follows deeds and 37 agrees with 972; 'commentators' is also wrong since Manakkudavar is absent and Kalaignar allegorises.

Own understanding prevails over study versus knowledge flows as one studies, and Parimelazhagar on 396 names 373 and says they do not collide where fate does not oppose; the note omits this explicit reconciliation.

On Manakkudavar's reading (the note names none) native understanding is low-rated in 404 and dominant in 373, which are compatible, and Parimelazhagar's 373 means fate-born folly, removing the pairing altogether.
454 says understanding merely seems one's own and has its root in one's company, against 373's own or fate-given understanding prevailing, two rival accounts of source on any of the readings.
356 says those who learned and saw reach release, which does not promise that learning always succeeds, so 373's fated limit leaves it standing and 'undercuts' overstates.

'Listening at once' misreports Parimelazhagar, who on 416 compares a little hearing to raindrops that gather, so it is cumulative, and Manakkudavar and Kalaignar give no instant gain; it also compares knowledge with greatness.
729 penalises a subset of the learned who will not speak in assembly, which qualifies 410 rather than opposing it, so the type should be qualifies.

Verse 2 asks what fruit learning has without worship, which Parimelazhagar takes as the end of scripture-knowledge, and 400 praises learning as imperishable wealth; these work at different levels and the thin note shows no incompatibility.

Parimelazhagar says on 423 to judge without regard to the speaker and on 415 that those without conduct are not to be heard, a real clash in his own reading, correctly cited; it bears on credibility more than on the thread's sources of understanding.

On Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's 850 what the high ones affirm may not be denied, while 423 discounts the speaker, a real clash on authority; the note rightly says Kalaignar's evidence gloss on 850 narrows the gap.

The face mirrors the heart in 706 while 824's enemies smile over hostility, and the note is right that Parimelazhagar's 824 calls the face the instrument of reading whose signal here fails; he does not reconcile them.

Parimelazhagar's 585 is about not spilling what is in mind under the four methods, mainly speech under pressure, while 706 is about the face showing feeling, so 'the spy's art should be impossible' overreads.

Love shows in tears (71) and enemies may weep falsely (828) are logically compatible, since 71 never says all tears show love, and 'trusts absolutely' is too strong, even though Parimelazhagar does call tears grounds for inference.

Within one chapter hostility is hidden even from the face (Parimelazhagar on 824) and an enemy's fine words are known at once (826), a real pull, though the channels differ (face versus speech) and the note names no commentator.

Ask if you find fit givers against not asking even the best being ten million times better is a direct opposition, but I could not find the note's 'edge of death' in Parimelazhagar on 1051 here, and his nearest is on 1055 and 1061.

Asking from the right person is like giving against nothing being more degrading than asking even water for a cow, a direct clash, and the note rightly points out that 1061 stops the choice of giver from dissolving it.

Taking is bad even if it were a road to heaven, against ask the worthy and any blame falls on the refuser, two opposed verdicts on receiving; the note's standpoint remark is the reconciliation, and it is the note's rather than a commentator's.
As the note itself says the standards differ: Parimelazhagar's 229 weighs lasting misery against begging's passing shame and 1066 ranks disgrace to the tongue, so the two scales do not collide.

Benevolence seeks no return against feeding as a depository that comes back to help the giver (Parimelazhagar, accurate), a real pull on motive though he adds 'for virtue's sake' at 226 and the verses concern ஒப்புரவு and ஈகை respectively.
222 denies that giving needs heaven and 231 names renown as life's gain, which do not conflict since 222 says nothing about fame, so 'for itself versus as gain' is imposed.

On Manakkudavar's reading, which the note names correctly, wealth is for the worthy while true giving is to those who lack and all else is like repayable lending; Parimelazhagar's 212 takes தக்கார் as the giver and removes this.
'Worth begging for' is an idiom of value (Manakkudavar: all would ask for it) with nothing to say about begging's disgrace, so only the root இர- is shared.

Same chapter: no leaving once befriended against leaving a fool's friendship is gain, a real pull, and the note is right that Parimelazhagar (at 797, 800) reconciles it by limiting exit to what was taken on unknowingly.

800 concerns unsuitable friends taken on unknowingly (Parimelazhagar) and 807 long-standing affection, different classes as the note half concedes, and its unsettled-boundary question is fair but is not a clash between these verses.

Parimelazhagar's 805 takes the folly as a lapse not of the friend's nature, while 797 concerns fools as such, so the difference is character rather than the note's 'only' age of the bond, and பேதைமை is merely shared.

Grows with practice against practice not needed, and Parimelazhagar does rank three causes with shared feeling first as stated, though growth versus origin eases the clash and 'plain tension' is somewhat strong.
785 concerns how friendship arises and 801 defines what makes it 'old', so a chapter's mere existence is no conflict, even though the note reports Parimelazhagar's 801 correctly.
கெழுதகைமை is truly shared, but a minister presuming on a king and a friend tolerating a friend are not 'the same bond', so it is a neat cross-domain parallel rather than a tension.

Rebuke a friend's excess against silently fading out those who feign inability concern different classes of friend, and the note's own last clause explains away the conflict, though Parimelazhagar gives a practical reason at 818.

Both use பேராண்மை, but Parimelazhagar on 148 says mastering the inner foe is greater even for those who master outer foes, which is an extension, so the graph's separate QUALIFIES edge is sound and this TENSION is not.
எஃகு is wealth as a weapon in 759 and a metaphor for the keenness of valour in 773, not rival claims to be the sharpest thing, so only a word is shared.
Chief of the king's assets and source of victory are different claims, and Parimelazhagar's 546 says the spear works when the sceptre is straight, so the 'two answers' dissolve on his reading.
The note is honest and correct on both commentators, and its own 'different questions' is right: force as best method when stronger and justice as ground of victory are compatible.

253 uses the weapon-holder only as a simile for the meat-eater's mind and does not assess warriors, so 'honours what it distrusts' reads doctrine into a comparison, although the two attitudes do differ.
A real parallel in form (days counted as wasted), with both glosses correct, but the verses do not exclude each other, so the type should be parallel_domain or same_image.

723 says dying among enemies is commoner than speaking fearlessly in assembly and 780 prizes a specific death, a rarity claim against a worth claim, and 780 deflates nothing, so 'each deflated by the other' is false.

thread:true_wealth.issue: Five of the six named holders rest on sound links; energy rests only on the weak 592-400, though the verse does say it. Overstated: 'keeps awarding' describes six verses of 1330. The commentators read each superlative against material wealth, so the verses rarely compete with each other on their own reading; only 751 versus 400 is a head-on clash. One sound link is a reversed duplicate. The note on 751-400 wrongly speaks of 'each book's register': both verses are in the Book of Wealth.

thread:competing_supremes.issue: Fails on restraint (32-122 is only a shared formula; restraint is a kind of virtue) and 92-225 is forced. The last sentence overreaches: 323 is an explicit ranking and Parimelazhagar treats it as settling the order, so not every superlative is mere praise.
thread:competing_supremes.corrected_claim: The formula recurs beyond wealth and sometimes collides: nothing surpasses virtue, yet nothing surpasses apt speech; nothing beats truth, yet not killing is ranked above it; poverty is unmatched pain, yet wealth under a tyrant hurts more. Commentators reconcile the first two, and 323 is a deliberate ranking, so these superlatives need case-by-case reading.

thread:ethics_vs_statecraft.issue: All five named areas have a sound link, though two links are the same pair. Overstated in three ways: 480 limits generosity rather than reversing it; 'often' for commentators' added limits rests on clear cases at 550 and 829; and Parimelazhagar directs 303 at renunciants, so some rules were not universal for him. Counterevidence against a book-wide pattern: 546 and 657 show the Book of Wealth upholding ethics.
thread:ethics_vs_statecraft.corrected_claim: Five rules stated without exception in the Book of Virtue meet specific verses in the Book of Wealth that suspend or limit them: killing, anger, hypocrisy, generosity and purity of mind. The verses do not acknowledge this; Parimelazhagar reconciles some by adding limits such as royal duty and enemies only. The Book of Wealth elsewhere upholds ethics (546, 657).

thread:love_overturns.issue: Of the four named examples only shame holds. Senses and warrior are contrasts without incompatibility, and backbiting is forced because அலர் is not புறங்கூறல். 'Overturns' is false as a claim about the book: these are dramatised speakers in stated situations, on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's framing, and do not revise the earlier teaching.
thread:love_overturns.corrected_claim: A few lover-speakers reuse the earlier books' language against its grain: shame worth dying for is set aside to save life (1132/1017), the body-soul bond called flimsy in 338 becomes the image of union (1122), and honour's ban on following those who slight you is called unavailable to the lovesick (1255/966). These are dramatised speeches and do not overturn the earlier teaching.

thread:gender_asymmetry.issue: Only shame and memory hold, and memory's gender contrast fails on Manakkudavar, who gives 1202 to the woman. Evening, night and leaving fail: most contrasts are union against separation, not man against woman, and two links lie outside the Book of Love. Counterevidence: 1251 has the woman's shame break, and the man suffers in 1132 and 1268. 1137, the verse that states the asymmetry outright, is not among the links.
thread:gender_asymmetry.corrected_claim: On Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments, the man and woman differ over shame (1132/1163) and memory (1202/1207), and 1137 states the first contrast outright. Manakkudavar assigns some speakers differently, and most other differences in the Book of Love follow union and separation rather than gender.

thread:truth_by_effect.issue: The second sentence holds (292-297). 'Not agreement with fact' is Parimelazhagar's explicit gloss on 291, not the verse's wording, and 291 appears only in a forced link, so most links do not test the claim. Counterevidence: 293 still treats lying as going against what one's own heart knows, in the same chapter.
thread:truth_by_effect.corrected_claim: On Parimelazhagar's reading, chapter 30 defines truthfulness by harmlessness of effect and explicitly sets aside mere statement of what happened, though 293 still treats lying as going against what one knows. That definition carries real weight: without it, 297's unbroken not-lying and 292's blameless falsehood would conflict.

thread:justice_of_the_world.issue: Promise, admission and protest hold (170, 210, 169, 1062, 377). Fails on verse 1, which makes no moral claim, and on 'explains misery as deserved' as an opposite of the protest (330-1062 weak). 'Without resolving them' holds for the verses only: Parimelazhagar resolves 169 and 170 through past deeds, and his 1062 keeps past deeds too. 169 may be hypothetical on his 'if they occur'.
thread:justice_of_the_world.corrected_claim: The Kural says the upright do not fall (170, 210), yet treats the prosperity of the crooked and ruin of the upright as a puzzle (169), and it both accepts the apportioner (377) and curses the world's maker if begging was decreed (1062). The verses leave this open; Parimelazhagar resolves it through past deeds.

thread:fate_and_agency.issue: Well supported by 371-620, 620-380, 609-371, 429-380 and 482-376. The closing point about தான் முந்துறும் is a true verbal echo but rests on a weak link and shows no conflict. 'Treat them as chosen' is strictest for 609 and 620. Parimelazhagar narrows the conflict at 620 and Manakkudavar at 429, which the claim doesn't mention.

thread:poverty.issue: 'Whether character survives poverty' holds (988-1044, 532-408). The first sentence is a word overlap for two different conditions, and 'householder' is not in the verses. 'Whether anything is worse' has no sound link here (657-1041 is not a clash), though 558 and 841 against 1041 in another thread do support it. Parimelazhagar's gloss at 532 largely eases the understanding clash.
thread:poverty.corrected_claim: The Kural disagrees with itself on whether worth survives poverty (988 against 1044) and on whether the world despises the poor (752 against 841). இன்மை also names the ascetic's chosen possessionlessness, but that is a different condition from destitution.

thread:birth_across_book.issue: Friends and integrity hold; officials (502) rest only on a weak link. 'Denied in one verse' is false: 409, in the thread's own links, also subordinates birth, and 133 redefines it by conduct. 'Usually quoted' cannot be checked from this corpus. On Parimelazhagar's reading 972 keeps varna work-differences, so it denies less than the thread implies.
thread:birth_across_book.corrected_claim: Besides denials of birth's rank (972; also 409 for learning), the book also treats birth as a real factor: integrity is natural to the well-born (951), friends are screened by family (793, 794) and birth is named as a source of courtesy (992). Quoting 972 alone gives a partial picture.

thread:knowing_and_learning.issue: Only study against fate or innate nature and against company hold. Hearing rests on the wrong 396-416, and poverty's absence has no link in this thread. The two sound links on 423 concern a speaker's credibility, not sources of understanding. Parimelazhagar explicitly reconciles 396 with 373, which the thread does not mention.
thread:knowing_and_learning.corrected_claim: The book names at least three sources of understanding that do not sit easily together: study (396), one's own or fated nature (373) and company (454). Parimelazhagar reconciles study with fate by limiting study's reach to where fate does not oppose it. Separately, it is divided on whether a speaker's standing matters (423, 415, 850).

thread:signs_and_faces.issue: The face and enemies' faces hold (706-824, 824-826). Spies and tears rest on weak links, and 'lovers feign indifference' has no link at all. 'Tears prove love' overstates 71: enemies' false tears do not contradict it.
thread:signs_and_faces.corrected_claim: The face is said to show the heart (706), yet enemies' smiles are said to hide hostility even from the face (824) while their words are soon seen through (826). Tears publish love in 71 and may conceal a weapon in 828, but those verses concern different people and do not conflict.

thread:giving_and_asking.issue: Holds on 1051-1061, 1054-1066, 222-1051 and 211-226. 'For itself' rests on 222 and 211. Fair to say the consecutive chapters open opposed. Caution: the note's 'edge of death' attribution at 1051-1061 was not found in the commentary available, and 780-1066 should go.

thread:limits_of_friendship.issue: 'A friend can't be left' against leaving a fool, and practice against no practice, hold, though the second is mild. 'Old friends may ruin you' is true of 807 but its clash with 800 is weak. The final sentence is speculative and partly wrong, since Parimelazhagar does state a limit at 800 (what one took on unknowingly) and 805 gives a character-versus-lapse distinction.
thread:limits_of_friendship.corrected_claim: The book says those devoted to friendship do not leave a friend (791) yet leaving a fool's friendship is gain (797), and says friendship grows with practice (783) yet does not need it (785). Parimelazhagar supplies the limit: exit is for what one took on unknowingly (800). Old friends who harm you are kept (807), which he treats as a separate case.

thread:manliness_contested.issue: No link survives as a tension. The strongest (773, 148) is an extension, already typed QUALIFIES, on Parimelazhagar's own account. The rest share a word (எஃகு), an image or a form. 'Contests' and 'each claim victory' describe an essay's arrangement, not a dispute in the verses.
